pomegranate-extract.text: Pomegranate extract is taken orally or applied in skincare by people who want antioxidant support for a clearer, more even complexion. Its ellagitannin content is well studied in the lab, while effects on skin appearance in people have not been confirmed.

aloe-leaf-extract.text: Aloe leaf extract is a staple of after-sun gels, moisturizers and facial products, used to soothe and hydrate skin so it looks calmer and smoother. Evidence on wound healing is mixed, and its effect on skin appearance specifically is lightly studied.

sugarcane-extract.text: Sugarcane extract is promoted as a natural, gentle source of glycolic acid for exfoliating dull skin and smoothing texture. Glycolic acid itself is well studied as an exfoliant, while the plant extract has not been tested for skin results.

apple-fruit-water.text: Apple fruit water appears in some creams as a mild source of fruit acids (AHAs) for gentle exfoliation and a fresher look. The evidence for this use is a single 2018 formulation study.

turmeric-root-extract.text: Turmeric root extract is used in skincare as a brightening and antioxidant ingredient, with users hoping for a more even, glowing complexion. Support for this use comes mainly from cell studies, with little human skin data.

menthyl-lactate.text: Menthyl lactate is a milder, longer-lasting cooling agent used in cosmetics, fragrances and oral-care products to give a fresh sensation. It is valued for feel in products, and no study has tested it for changes in how skin looks.

exosome-serums.text: Exosome serums are promoted for skin regeneration and rejuvenation, often applied after microneedling to speed recovery and improve texture. The biology is promising in the lab, while published human skin data remain very limited.

mesenchymal-stem-cell-conditioned-media.text: Stem-cell conditioned media appear in serums and post-procedure treatments marketed for skin regeneration and rejuvenation. The idea draws on lab findings about the growth factors they contain, and human evidence so far is limited to early-phase trials.

fibroblast-growth-factor-fgf.text: Topical FGF is added to some anti-aging serums on the strength of its role in wound repair, with the aim of firmer, smoother-looking skin. It is well studied in wound healing, and human cosmetic trials for wrinkles were not found.

anagain.text: Anagain is a pea-sprout cosmetic ingredient in hair-growth serums, discussed alongside Redensyl, Capixyl and Baicapil by people seeking fuller hair. Support is a small 10-person gene-expression study.

baicapil.text: Baicapil is a branded cosmetic active in scalp serums aimed at thinning hair, with its name pointing to baicalin from skullcap. People use it hoping for less shedding and denser-looking hair, and no trial of the product itself was found.

dihydroquercetin-glucoside.text: DHQG is one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic hair-growth active used in serums by people with thinning hair. The component has not been studied on its own for hair, and the claims rest on Redensyl marketing data.

egcg-glucoside.text: EGCG-glucoside is the green-tea-derived partner of DHQG in Redensyl, a cosmetic hair-growth active used for thinning hair. EGCG has wider research, and hair data on this component alone are lacking.

biochanin-a.text: Biochanin A is a red-clover phytoestrogen named as a component of Capixyl, a cosmetic hair-growth active used on thinning scalp hair. It has been studied for other purposes, and hair studies on the compound itself were not found.

chain: Follicle stem cells switch to growth
suvomipic.text: Suvomipic (PP405) is an experimental once-daily topical from Pelage Pharmaceuticals that hair-loss followers watch as a possible new regrowth option. It is in phase 2, with early results reported by the company.

quercitrin.text: Quercitrin is a plant flavonoid sometimes floated in hair-health discussions for its antioxidant properties. Antioxidant lab data exist, and hair studies in people were not found.

horsetail-extract.text: Horsetail extract is sold in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a silica source, with users hoping for stronger, fuller hair. Lab data are limited and single-ingredient hair trials were not found.

isoflavones.text: Soy isoflavones such as genistein and daidzein come up in hair discussions because of their estrogen-like activity, with some users hoping for less thinning. They have been studied in people for other conditions rather than for hair.

estrogen-topical-for-hair.text: Scalp estrogen solutions, mainly alfatradiol sold in Germany and parts of Latin America, are used for pattern hair loss to slow thinning. Trials suggest benefit in some regions of the scalp, and regrowth has not been shown.

triamcinolone-injections.text: Dermatologists inject triamcinolone into patches of alopecia areata to regrow hair, and most treated patients have reported regrowth. It treats an autoimmune condition and is not used for ordinary pattern hair loss.

deuruxolitinib.text: Deuruxolitinib (Leqselvi) is an oral drug approved in the US for severe alopecia areata, and people with extensive hair loss follow it for full regrowth. Trials showed strong regrowth, and it is not indicated for pattern baldness.

ruxolitinib-oral.text: Oral ruxolitinib is approved for blood and transplant conditions and is investigational for alopecia areata, where it is followed as an off-label route to regrowth. Hair evidence comes from smaller studies.

methotrexate-for-alopecia.text: Methotrexate is tried off-label for alopecia areata, alone or with corticosteroids, to regrow hair lost to autoimmune attack. Small studies and a 2019 meta-analysis exist, with definitive evidence described as scarce.

mometasone.text: Mometasone is a steroid used for allergies, asthma and eczema, and it comes up in hair discussions through scalp inflammation and relatives used in alopecia areata. Hair-loss studies of it were not found.

diaminopyrimidine-oxide.text: Diaminopyrimidine oxide appears in hair-growth lotions and shampoos as a minoxidil-related cosmetic ingredient for people with thinning hair. It is known mainly from cosmetic patents, and trials were not found.

chain: Follicle energy and cell support claimed
sarcosine-hair.text: Sarcosine is listed as a component in some hair-growth blends, with the idea that it supports follicle cells. Hair studies behind it were not found.

chain: Ceylon cinnamon bark in a blend
cinnamomum-zeylanicum-bark-extract.text: Ceylon cinnamon bark extract appears in the cosmetic blend Sepicontrol A5 and is mentioned in hair-care product discussions. No hair or scalp studies were found for it.

hydroxypropyl-ammonium-gluconate.text: This gluconate salt is paired with a gluconamide in bond-building hair products promoted for strengthening fibres and reducing breakage. The only research found is crystal chemistry, and the mechanism on hair was described as unknown.

hydrolyzed-silk-protein.text: Hydrolyzed silk protein is added to conditioners so hair feels softer and looks glossier after use. Hair trials of the ingredient were not found.

hydrolyzed-keratin.text: Hydrolyzed keratin is added to conditioners and repair products to strengthen and smooth damaged hair for a healthier look. Hair-specific human data are scarce.
